messages.content: I want to develop simultaneous speech translation that preserves late-resolved negation and semantic roles even while it commits output irreversibly under bounded latency.

The central difficulty is that the translation must begin before the full utterance is available, yet an emitted word cannot later be taken back. A later part of the speech may establish whether a statement was negated or clarify who did what to whom. The goal is to preserve those meanings without waiting indefinitely to produce output.
What would count as success here? I want the accuracy target stated alongside the timing and overall-quality constraints.

The target is at least 20% fewer negation and semantic-role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline. At the same time, average lagging must stay below two seconds, and overall COMET must not decrease relative to that same baseline. These are simultaneous requirements, not alternatives: a gain on the targeted errors alone would not satisfy the goal if it came with too much lag or lower overall COMET.
Does “20% fewer” mean 20 percentage points fewer?

No. “At least 20% fewer” expresses a relative reduction against the matched-latency streaming baseline, not necessarily a difference of 20 percentage points. The wording does not supply a baseline error value, so it does not imply any particular absolute error count or rate.
Why call out late-resolved negation separately from translation quality in general?

Because an early stretch of speech can appear to support one reading, while later speech determines that the intended meaning is negative. If the translation has already irreversibly asserted the positive reading, the later information cannot simply be used to replace it. The goal highlights preserving that distinction specifically; overall COMET remains a separate quality constraint.
And by semantic roles, do you mean keeping the participants’ relationships intact rather than merely retaining their words?

Yes. Semantic roles concern relationships such as who performs an action and who receives it. The relevant error is not just omitting a word: an output could contain the right participants yet convey the wrong relationship between them. Here, role preservation matters even when the speech that resolves those relationships arrives after an output decision has to be made.
Could the system meet the meaning goal by waiting until every ambiguity is settled?

Not if that pushes average lagging to two seconds or more. The goal explicitly combines meaning preservation with average lagging below two seconds and irreversible output under bounded latency. Waiting is therefore not an unrestricted escape from the risk of an early commitment.
I also don’t want “irreversible” to be interpreted as permission to make an early guess and silently fix it later.

That is the right distinction. Under an irreversible-output requirement, later text cannot erase or replace what was already committed. Subsequent output may continue the translation, but success cannot depend on retroactively changing an earlier assertion that got negation or a semantic role wrong.
What exactly is the comparison for the error reduction?

It is a matched-latency streaming baseline. The stated aim is to have at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than that baseline while operating under the latency requirement. The comparison for overall COMET is also against the same baseline; the goal does not switch to a different reference for the quality condition.
If overall COMET stays level but the targeted errors improve, is that compatible with the goal?

Yes, provided the improvement reaches at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than the matched-latency streaming baseline and average lagging remains below two seconds. “Without reducing overall COMET” allows an unchanged overall COMET score relative to that baseline; it does not demand an increase.
Conversely, could a higher COMET score compensate for missing the negation-and-role target?

No. The error reduction is an explicit requirement in its own right. A higher overall COMET score would not turn a smaller-than-20% reduction in negation and role errors into satisfaction of that requirement. The same applies in reverse: reaching the targeted reduction would not compensate for reduced overall COMET or average lagging that is not below two seconds.
Is two seconds inclusive?
No. “Below two seconds” is a strict threshold for average lagging. An average lagging of exactly two seconds would not meet that wording, even if the other requirements were satisfied.
Can I read this as a goal, rather than a report that these results have already been obtained?

Yes. It specifies what the simultaneous speech translation should achieve: preserve late-resolved negation and semantic roles during irreversible, bounded-latency output; produce at least 20% fewer errors of those kinds than the matched-latency streaming baseline; keep average lagging below two seconds; and avoid reducing overall COMET relative to that same baseline. It does not state that an experiment has already met those conditions or prescribe a particular implementation.
So the central tension is between committing promptly and not committing to a meaning that later speech overturns?

Exactly. Prompt, irreversible output creates the risk; late clarification of negation or semantic roles makes that risk consequential. The goal is to handle that tension while satisfying all three stated comparisons and limits: the targeted error reduction, average lagging below two seconds, and no drop in overall COMET against the same streaming baseline.
How might we address the risk of committing to a translation before negation or semantic roles are clear?

One proposal is to use source-conditioned role–polarity lattices together with a 1.5-second adaptive commit gate. The system would emit only prefixes that remain invariant across plausible continuations of the source speech. That makes stability across those continuations the condition for an irreversible commitment.
What work is the role–polarity lattice doing in that description?

It represents possibilities that matter for who did what to whom—the roles—and whether the meaning is positive or negative—the polarity. Calling it source-conditioned means those possibilities are considered in light of the source speech available so far. The proposal is to avoid committing output that depends on a role or polarity distinction the source has not yet resolved.
Does a lattice mean choosing one interpretation early and keeping alternatives only as a backup?

No. The point of retaining plausible alternatives is to test what can be said without choosing prematurely among them. If an output prefix would change depending on which plausible continuation arrives, it is not invariant and would not be emitted under the proposed rule.
Can you explain “invariant prefix” without assuming a particular language pair?

It is an initial portion of the translation that can be committed without needing to revise it when any of the plausible source continuations arrives. For example, if those continuations would require different claims about whether an action happened, a prefix that already asserts one of those claims would not be invariant. An earlier prefix that does not make that disputed commitment might be.
So the prefix has to be safe as output, not just contain words that look similar across alternatives?

Right. The relevant question is whether emitting that prefix would preserve the intended role and polarity under the plausible continuations, not whether isolated words happen to resemble one another. An irreversible prefix should not smuggle in a claim that one continuation would overturn.
Where does the 1.5-second adaptive commit gate fit?

It is the proposed timing component governing when to commit output, alongside the invariance condition. “Adaptive” indicates that commitment is responsive to what can safely be emitted as the source unfolds, rather than simply emitting each candidate prefix as soon as it appears. The proposal names a 1.5-second gate; it does not, by itself, specify all the gate’s operating rules.
Should I interpret 1.5 seconds as a guaranteed average lagging figure?

No. The 1.5 seconds describes the proposed adaptive commit gate, not a measured average lagging result. Nor does naming the gate establish that the broader latency and quality goals have been achieved. Those would require evidence beyond this proposal.
What if the plausible continuations still disagree after the gate’s interval?

The proposal gives no explicit fallback rule for that case. Its stated emission rule is to output only prefixes invariant across plausible continuations. We should not infer that the gate permits a non-invariant guess, or that it guarantees an invariant prefix will become available within 1.5 seconds.
Is the method saying to withhold an entire translation whenever one part is uncertain?

Not necessarily. It says to emit only prefixes that are invariant. A usable initial prefix could be committed even while a later role or polarity decision remains unresolved; what cannot be committed is a prefix whose correctness depends on settling that unresolved distinction. The proposal does not specify how often either situation occurs.
Why condition the lattice on the source rather than treat every conceivable continuation as equally relevant?

The proposal concerns plausible continuations of the source speech, not arbitrary possibilities detached from it. Conditioning on the source keeps the stability test tied to what has actually been heard. It does not specify a particular way to define or rank plausibility.
Does this proposal require the system to predict the final sentence correctly before speaking?

No. It aims to find what is already safe to say across plausible ways the source might continue. That differs from committing to one predicted full sentence. The lattice keeps relevant role and polarity alternatives in view, while the gate controls commitment of a prefix that survives those alternatives.
Could a prefix be invariant now but become unsafe when an unexpected continuation arrives?

The stated criterion is invariance across *plausible* continuations, not a guarantee against every imaginable continuation. The proposal does not claim perfect foresight. Its intended protection is against premature commitments where the continuations being considered would change the output.
What is the specific connection between this approach and irreversible output?

Because an emitted prefix cannot be taken back, the proposal checks it before emission rather than relying on later correction. The role–polarity lattice exposes distinctions that may still matter, and the adaptive gate permits commitment only of a prefix invariant across the plausible continuations under consideration.
And the proposal itself doesn’t say whether this is already better than a streaming baseline?

Correct. It specifies an approach, not a result. It does not report an error reduction, average lagging, or COMET outcome. Its connection to the broader goal is the proposed way of handling late-resolved roles and negation while making bounded-latency, irreversible commitments.
That leaves me with the key question: how can the decoder identify irreversible target prefixes that survive late-arriving negators and role disambiguation within the 1.5-second gate?

The proposed role–polarity lattice provides the setting for that question, but it does not answer it on its own. The decoder would need to distinguish a prefix that remains valid across plausible continuations from one that only looks safe because the source has not yet revealed a negator or clarified the roles. How to make that distinction in time for the 1.5-second gate is the unresolved issue.
What does it mean for a target prefix to “survive” a late-arriving negator?

It means the already-emitted prefix would still be an appropriate beginning of the translation after that negator is taken into account. If the later negator would require changing what the prefix asserted, the prefix has not survived. Since output is irreversible, adding words later is not the same as taking back an earlier contradictory commitment.
Is the role-disambiguation problem analogous?

Yes. A later part of the source may establish which participant has which role. A target prefix survives only if it remains appropriate under that clarification. A prefix that has already committed to the wrong relationship between participants cannot be made safe merely by continuing the translation.
Could the decoder just look for a shared beginning among the candidate translations?

A shared beginning is relevant, but the question is whether it is genuinely safe to commit. The decoder must not mistake superficial agreement at the start of candidate output for agreement about a role or polarity claim that the prefix already conveys. The node asks how to identify prefixes that survive the later information, not simply how to find matching initial words.
So a prefix can be problematic even before it explicitly says “not”?

Potentially, yes. What matters is the meaning the committed prefix conveys in context. If it already commits the translation to an affirmative reading that a late negator would overturn, withholding the word “not” does not by itself make that earlier commitment safe. The question is whether the whole emitted prefix can stand unchanged.
How should I understand “irreversible target prefix” here?

It is an initial stretch of target-language output that the decoder commits and cannot revise. That is why the survival test matters before emission: the decoder cannot rely on editing the prefix after the source resolves negation or semantic roles.
Does the question assume that every uncertainty can be resolved inside 1.5 seconds?

No. It asks how identification can work within the 1.5-second gate; it does not state that the source always resolves negation or roles during that interval, or that a safe prefix will always be available. Those possibilities are part of what makes the question difficult.
If the source has not resolved a role, what would the decoder be looking for?

Conceptually, it would be looking for an initial target stretch that remains appropriate under the plausible role assignments still in play. If the alternatives require different commitments at the start, the proposed invariance rule does not justify emitting one of them as though the role were settled. The open question is how the decoder recognizes that distinction promptly enough.
And for polarity, it has to consider that a negator might arrive after an apparently affirmative beginning?

Exactly. The point is not to treat the current absence of a negator as proof of positive polarity when a plausible continuation could supply one. The decoder needs to know whether the target prefix would remain valid in either case, insofar as those continuations remain plausible.
Does “plausible” mean guarding against every logically possible future utterance?

No. The proposal refers to plausible continuations conditioned on the source speech. The question inherits that framing. It does not define a particular plausibility rule, so it would be premature to claim exactly which continuations the decoder includes or excludes.
Is there a distinction between recognizing a safe prefix and deciding when to release it?

Yes. Identifying a prefix that survives the relevant continuations concerns its suitability for irreversible output. The 1.5-second adaptive commit gate concerns the timing of commitment. The question brings them together: can the decoder establish that suitability within the gate, rather than merely finding a safe prefix after the opportunity to commit promptly has passed?
What if there is a common beginning, but it only stays common until a later part forces different wording?

The committed beginning would have to remain valid when that later wording differs. Divergence after the committed prefix is not itself a problem; a later need to alter the committed prefix is. That is the practical boundary the word “survive” is trying to capture.
Would it be accurate to phrase the question as: how does the decoder tell what can be said now without predetermining negation or who did what to whom?

Yes, with two important qualifications: the answer must concern an *irreversible target prefix*, and the identification has to fit within the *1.5-second gate*. Those qualifications keep the focus on safe commitment under the proposed timing constraint, rather than on eventually producing a correct translation once all the source speech is available.
Are we claiming the lattice and gate already solve that identification problem?

No. They frame the proposed approach, while this node poses the identification problem explicitly. It does not give a decoder procedure or establish that prefixes surviving late negation and role disambiguation can always be found within the 1.5-second gate.
Here’s a hypothesis about the decoder question: within the 1.5-second gate, committing prefixes shared across a calibrated 95%-mass lattice yields at least 97% role–polarity prefix correctness.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis, not an established result. It proposes using agreement across a calibrated lattice covering 95% of the assigned mass as the basis for irreversible prefix commitments within the 1.5-second gate. The predicted outcome is role–polarity prefix correctness of at least 97%.
What does “shared across” add? Why not commit the prefix of whichever continuation currently looks most likely?

“Shared across” makes agreement the criterion rather than selecting a single favored continuation. A prefix qualifies under the hypothesis when it is common to the alternatives included in the calibrated 95%-mass lattice. That is intended to avoid committing to wording that depends on an unresolved role or polarity choice within those alternatives.
Does the 95% figure mean the emitted prefixes themselves are expected to be 95% correct?

No. The figures describe different things. The 95% specifies the mass covered by the calibrated lattice used to assess shared prefixes. The at-least-97% figure is the hypothesized role–polarity correctness of the committed prefixes. Neither percentage can simply be substituted for the other.
And the word “calibrated” matters, rather than this being any collection of continuations?

Yes. The hypothesis specifically calls for a *calibrated* 95%-mass lattice. That qualification matters to the proposed link between agreement within the lattice and the predicted correctness. The statement does not specify how calibration is performed or demonstrate that it has been achieved.
If every prefix in that 95%-mass lattice agrees, is the hypothesis claiming certainty that later speech cannot contradict it?

No. Agreement within a 95%-mass lattice is not the same as agreement with every possible continuation. The hypothesis predicts at least 97% role–polarity prefix correctness for commitments made this way; it does not promise that each committed prefix will survive every late-arriving negator or role clarification.
Does it say the lattice will always contain a shared prefix worth emitting within 1.5 seconds?

No. The hypothesis concerns the correctness of prefixes committed by this rule within the 1.5-second gate. It does not state how frequently a qualifying prefix exists, how long such prefixes are, or whether one is available for every segment of speech.
Could someone mistake the 1.5-second gate for a measured average lagging result?

They could, but that would overstate the claim. Here 1.5 seconds identifies the gate within which the proposed commitments occur. The hypothesis does not report measured average lagging or establish that any separate latency target has been met.
I want to keep the role and polarity part explicit. What exactly is the predicted correctness about?

It is about the role–polarity correctness of the *committed target prefixes*: whether those irreversible beginnings preserve the relevant relationships between participants and the relevant positive or negative meaning. The hypothesis is not a claim that entire completed translations are at least 97% correct, nor does it state an overall translation-quality score.
If a later negator appears, is that precisely the kind of event this hypothesis is meant to withstand?

Yes. Late-arriving negation and later role disambiguation motivate checking for prefixes shared across the lattice. The hypothesis is that applying that check within the gate yields the stated level of role–polarity prefix correctness. It remains a prediction, so the statement does not establish how often a late negator or role clarification would actually be handled correctly.
Suppose alternatives agree on a few opening words but disagree about who acted. Is shared wording alone enough for the claimed kind of correctness?

The hypothesis concerns *role–polarity prefix correctness*, so a superficially shared string would not suffice if committing it already conveyed an incorrect role or polarity. The intended commitment is a prefix shared across the lattice that remains appropriate with respect to those meanings. The hypothesis does not spell out a separate procedure for checking semantic equivalence beyond the stated lattice-based rule.
Is the at-least-97% threshold a comparison against the streaming baseline?

No comparison to a baseline is stated in this hypothesis. The at-least-97% figure is an absolute predicted threshold for role–polarity prefix correctness under the proposed lattice-and-gate condition. It does not, on its own, establish a relative error reduction against another system.
Can we infer overall COMET from that prefix-correctness number?

No. Role–polarity correctness of committed prefixes and overall COMET are different assessments. This hypothesis gives a predicted threshold for the former; it supplies no COMET result or relationship that would let us calculate the latter.
So the concise reading is: use the calibrated 95%-mass lattice to find shared prefixes, commit them within the 1.5-second gate, and hypothesize at least 97% role–polarity prefix correctness?

Yes. That preserves the condition, the timing, and the predicted outcome without treating the hypothesis as a demonstrated result. It also leaves open the particulars the statement does not provide, such as how calibration or correctness would be assessed.

To evaluate the prefix-correctness hypothesis, let’s measure 95%-mass lattice prefix role–polarity correctness, AL, and COMET on 600 CoVoST2 Japanese–English utterances, against matched-latency baselines with 1.5-second gates.

That sets out an evaluation activity, not a result. The 600 CoVoST2 Japanese–English utterances are the specified material; the measurements are correctness of prefixes committed using the 95%-mass lattice, AL, and COMET. The comparisons are against matched-latency baselines with 1.5-second gates.
Why measure all three rather than just check whether the prefixes get the roles and polarity right?

Prefix role–polarity correctness addresses the specific meaning risk behind the hypothesis: an irreversible prefix should not misstate negation or who did what to whom. AL addresses timing, and COMET addresses overall translation quality. Measuring all three keeps a result on the targeted prefixes from standing in for evidence about latency or overall quality.
AL here means average lagging, correct?
Correct. AL is average lagging. It is the timing measure named in this activity; the activity does not provide an observed AL value.
Is the unit of analysis 600 utterances or 600 committed prefixes?

The specified material is 600 utterances, not a stated number of committed prefixes. Prefix role–polarity correctness is one of the measurements to make on that material. The activity does not say how many prefixes will be committed or prescribe a count of prefixes per utterance.
And CoVoST2 Japanese–English identifies the speech-translation material, not a claimed finding about that language pair?
Exactly. It identifies the named dataset and translation direction for the 600 utterances in this activity. No correctness, AL, or COMET outcome for them is supplied.
How does this evaluate the claim about a calibrated 95%-mass lattice and at least 97% correctness?

The earlier hypothesis predicts at least 97% role–polarity correctness for prefixes shared across a calibrated 95%-mass lattice and committed within a 1.5-second gate. Measuring 95%-mass lattice prefix role–polarity correctness on these utterances is the directly relevant observation. The activity does not report the observation or specify the calibration procedure.
Would an overall COMET score of 97% be the thing to look for?

No. The at-least-97% prediction concerns role–polarity *prefix correctness*, not COMET. COMET is measured separately. Treating a COMET value as though it were the prefix-correctness percentage would conflate two different quantities.
What does comparing against matched-latency baselines contribute?

It makes the comparison sensitive to the fact that delaying output can affect how much source speech is available before a commitment. The activity calls for matched-latency baselines with 1.5-second gates, so the lattice-prefix measurements are considered alongside baselines under the specified timing comparison. It does not name the baseline systems or give their scores.
Does saying the baselines are matched-latency already establish that their measured AL values will be identical?

No. “Matched-latency” describes the intended comparison, while AL is expressly something to measure. We should not turn that description into an unreported numerical equality or assume an observed AL outcome.
Is the 1.5-second gate the same as an AL of 1.5 seconds?
No. The 1.5 seconds specifies the gate in this activity. AL is a separate measured timing quantity. The gate value alone does not determine the AL result.
When you say ‘prefix correctness,’ are we evaluating a complete translation after the whole utterance is heard?

No. The named correctness measure is specifically about the prefixes committed from the 95%-mass lattice and their role–polarity meaning. COMET is the separately named overall-quality measure. The activity does not define a formal correctness rubric or replace the prefix assessment with an assessment of complete translations.
Could we infer how often the gate finds a prefix that can be emitted from these measurements?

Not from the activity as stated. It names prefix role–polarity correctness, AL, and COMET, but does not specify a separate measurement of how often a qualifying prefix is available or how long emitted prefixes are. Those quantities should not be presented as reported outcomes here.
What if correctness looks strong but timing or overall quality looks weak?

The three measurements would let those dimensions be considered separately. Strong prefix role–polarity correctness would not itself establish favorable AL or COMET, just as an AL or COMET result would not establish prefix correctness. At this stage, there are no values to characterize as strong or weak.
Does this activity by itself show the system has achieved the broader speech-translation goal?

No. It specifies what to measure on 600 CoVoST2 Japanese–English utterances and what baselines to compare against. Without observed correctness, AL, and COMET values, it establishes neither the hypothesis’s predicted correctness nor satisfaction of broader accuracy, latency, or quality requirements.
Do we know which matched-latency baselines are included or how the 600 utterances were selected?

Those details are not specified. The activity identifies matched-latency baselines with 1.5-second gates and a set of 600 CoVoST2 Japanese–English utterances, but does not name baseline implementations or describe utterance selection.
So I should describe the activity as measuring three distinct outcomes on the stated material, rather than as an experiment that has already verified the hypothesis?

Yes. The faithful description is to measure 95%-mass lattice prefix role–polarity correctness, average lagging, and COMET on 600 CoVoST2 Japanese–English utterances against matched-latency baselines with 1.5-second gates. Whether the measurements support the at-least-97% prefix-correctness hypothesis remains an open empirical question.
What did the measurements show on the 600 Japanese–English CoVoST2 utterances?
The 1.5-second-gated prefixes reached 97.4% role–polarity correctness, versus 94.0% for the baseline. Average lagging, or AL, was 1.8 seconds. COMET was 78.3, versus 78.1 for the baseline.
Can you separate those comparisons? I don’t want the timing number to be mistaken for another baseline difference.

Certainly. Prefix role–polarity correctness has an explicit comparison: 97.4% for the 1.5-second-gated prefixes versus 94.0% for the baseline. COMET also has an explicit comparison: 78.3 versus 78.1. AL is reported as 1.8 seconds, without a baseline AL value in this evidence.
How large is the prefix-correctness difference in percentage points?
It is 3.4 percentage points: 97.4% minus 94.0%. That is a difference between correctness percentages, not a claim about the number of individual prefixes or the number of utterances with errors.
And how should I describe the COMET difference?

The reported COMET value is 0.2 higher than the baseline’s: 78.3 versus 78.1. The figures give the direction and size of the observed difference, but do not provide an uncertainty estimate or establish how much of a practical difference it represents.
Does the 97.4% mean every one of the 600 utterances had a correct committed prefix?

No. The 600 figure counts the Japanese–English CoVoST2 utterances used for the evaluation, while 97.4% is the reported role–polarity correctness of the gated prefixes. It is not a claim that every utterance, every prefix, or every completed translation was correct.
Why keep saying ‘role–polarity prefix correctness’ instead of just ‘translation accuracy’?

Because the reported 97.4% and 94.0% concern a specific assessment of committed prefixes: whether they preserve roles and polarity. They are not presented as percentages for the accuracy of entire translations. COMET is reported separately as an overall translation-quality measure.
Could I say the gate was 1.8 seconds, since that’s the measured lag?
No. The prefixes were gated at 1.5 seconds; 1.8 seconds is the reported AL. The gate setting and average lagging are different quantities, so neither should be substituted for the other.
Do these figures tell us the baseline’s lag?
No baseline AL number appears in the reported evidence. We can state the observed AL of 1.8 seconds, but cannot calculate a numerical AL difference from the baseline using these figures alone.
Does a higher correctness percentage establish that late negators and role ambiguities were all handled correctly?

No. The 97.4% figure is an aggregate role–polarity prefix-correctness result, not a guarantee about each late-arriving negator or each instance of role disambiguation. The evidence does not give separate outcomes for those cases.
Is 94.0% the baseline’s COMET score?

No. The baseline’s role–polarity prefix correctness is 94.0%. Its reported COMET is 78.1. Keeping the metric names attached to the numbers is important because the two comparisons measure different things.
What, exactly, is the population behind the reported numbers?

The evidence identifies 600 Japanese–English CoVoST2 utterances. It does not specify the number of committed prefixes, a breakdown by utterance, or results for other datasets or translation directions. The reported figures should be read in that stated evaluation setting.
Can I infer a statistical confidence interval from 97.4% and the 600 utterances?

Not from those facts alone. The evidence does not state how many prefixes were assessed, how observations were grouped within utterances, or any uncertainty analysis. The reported percentage and the utterance count should not be turned into an unsupported confidence interval.
If I present the result in one sentence, how do I avoid overstating it?

You could say: ‘On 600 Japanese–English CoVoST2 utterances, 1.5-second-gated prefixes achieved 97.4% role–polarity correctness versus 94.0% for the baseline, with AL of 1.8 seconds and COMET of 78.3 versus 78.1.’ That reports the measurements and their stated comparisons without claiming additional outcomes.
What should we decide about the 95%-mass, 1.5-second gate?
Retain it for broader testing. The stated reason is that prefix correctness exceeds 97%, while AL and COMET meet their constraints.
Is “retain” a decision to use it definitively, or to keep evaluating it?
It is a decision to keep the 95%-mass, 1.5-second gate for broader testing. It does not say that broader testing has been completed or that the gate is definitively adopted for every setting.
I want to be precise about the reason. Which result is above 97%?

It is prefix correctness—specifically, the role–polarity correctness of committed prefixes in this context. The decision says that correctness *exceeds* 97%; it does not say that overall translation quality or COMET exceeds 97%.
Does “exceeds 97%” include exactly 97%?
No. “Exceeds 97%” means greater than 97%, not equal to it. That is the threshold stated as part of the reason for retaining the gate.
And the 95% in “95%-mass” is a different percentage?

Yes. The 95% describes the mass of the lattice used for deciding which prefixes to commit. The greater-than-97% statement concerns the correctness of those committed prefixes. They should not be described as two estimates of the same quantity.
How does the 1.5 seconds figure into the decision?
It identifies the gate being retained: the 95%-mass, 1.5-second gate. It is not itself the AL result. The decision separately states that AL meets its constraint.
Can you spell out the AL and COMET constraints without turning them into new measurements?

The relevant AL constraint is average lagging below two seconds, and the COMET constraint is no reduction in overall COMET relative to the same baseline used for comparison. The decision says those constraints are met; it does not provide new AL or COMET values.
Why mention both AL and COMET when the reason also cites prefix correctness?

Because they cover different requirements. Prefix correctness addresses whether irreversible output preserves role and polarity. AL addresses how promptly output is produced, while COMET addresses overall translation quality. The decision rests on the stated correctness threshold together with the two constraints, not on treating one measure as a substitute for the others.
Does this decision claim that broader testing will produce the same correctness?
No. Broader testing is what the gate is being retained *for*. The decision does not predict a correctness percentage, AL, or COMET result in those further tests.
Does it specify what broader testing consists of?
No. It does not name additional data, languages, baselines, or procedures. The scope of the decision is to retain the specified gate for broader testing, for the stated reasons.
Can I say that meeting AL and COMET constraints proves every aspect of the broader goal?

That would go beyond this decision. It says AL and COMET meet their constraints and prefix correctness exceeds 97%. It does not make a separate claim about every other target or about performance in broader testing.
Would it be fair to describe this as a cautious decision rather than a claim of universal reliability?
Yes. Retaining the 95%-mass, 1.5-second gate for broader testing acknowledges the stated correctness, AL, and COMET conditions while leaving its performance in broader settings open.
Give me the decision in one sentence, with its reason intact.
Retain the 95%-mass, 1.5-second gate for broader testing because role–polarity prefix correctness exceeds 97% and AL and COMET meet their constraints.
For the next phase, I want to work with the retained 1.5-second gate: calibrate the 95%-mass lattices by clause type, then test invariant-prefix commits on late-negation and role-swap subsets.

That is a plan for more focused testing. The gate remains at 1.5 seconds; the planned calibration distinguishes clause types when constructing the 95%-mass lattices. The planned tests then focus on whether invariant prefixes can be committed when late negation or a role swap makes an early interpretation risky. No outcomes from those tests are stated yet.
What does “by clause type” qualify here?

It qualifies calibration of the 95%-mass lattices. Rather than describing one undifferentiated calibration across all clauses, the plan calls for calibration that takes clause type into account. It does not identify the clause-type categories or specify how their calibration will be carried out.
Does that mean each clause type gets a different mass target?
Not as stated. The target remains a 95%-mass lattice. Calibrating by clause type does not, by itself, authorize changing the 95% figure or assigning new targets to particular types.
And are we changing the commit gate when we do that calibration?
No change to the gate is specified. The plan explicitly works with the retained 1.5-second gate. Calibration of the lattices and the timing of the gate are distinct parts of the plan.
How do the two planned activities fit together?

First, the plan calls for calibrating 95%-mass lattices by clause type. It then calls for testing invariant-prefix commitments on the late-negation and role-swap subsets with the retained gate. The calibration concerns the possibilities considered when judging a prefix; the testing concerns commits made under that setup. The statement does not prescribe a more detailed workflow.
What exactly are we trying to protect against in the late-negation subset?

The concern is that a negator arriving late could make an already-committed target prefix convey the wrong polarity. Testing invariant-prefix commits on that subset focuses on whether a prefix committed before that information arrives remains appropriate afterward. The plan does not say how many such cases there are or how they will perform.
And what does “role-swap” mean in the scope of this plan?

It points to cases where the assignment of semantic roles is at issue—where an early commitment could convey the wrong relationship between participants when the roles become clear. The plan names a role-swap subset for testing; it does not define its selection rule or claim that any particular role-swap case is already handled correctly.
Is an invariant prefix just one that can be followed by either of two different endings?

It must do more than allow different endings. The committed beginning itself must remain valid across the plausible continuations being considered. Could we approach irreversible commitments through the wording of the target output? I propose clause-aware reordering that emits role-neutral lead-ins, delaying polarity and agent–patient commitments under a 1.8-second lag budget.

That proposal shifts attention to what the translation can say before the clause has resolved its meaning. A role-neutral lead-in would let output begin without yet assigning who acted and who was affected. Clause-aware reordering would postpone wording that commits to those agent–patient roles or to positive versus negative polarity, while operating under the proposed 1.8-second lag budget.
What does “clause-aware” contribute, as opposed to simply delaying any risky word?

It makes the proposed ordering sensitive to the clause whose meaning is unfolding. The point is not merely to hold back an isolated word: a lead-in must remain appropriate as the clause later resolves its polarity and participant roles. The proposal does not specify a clause analysis procedure or rules for reordering.
Does a role-neutral lead-in mean an opening that leaves out every participant?

Not necessarily. It means the opening does not prematurely commit to the agent–patient relationship. The proposal does not require omitting all participants, nor does it prescribe a particular form for the lead-in. What matters is avoiding an early role assignment that later source speech could overturn.
Could the lead-in already say whether the event occurred, while leaving the participants’ roles open?

That could still commit to polarity. This proposal delays *both* polarity and agent–patient commitments. A lead-in would need to avoid asserting a positive reading if a later negator could require a negative one, even if the roles were left unspecified.
So there are two distinct sorts of meaning the early wording should avoid fixing?

Yes. Polarity concerns whether the clause is negated; agent–patient roles concern who acts and who is affected. The proposed lead-in is meant to defer commitments on both where they remain unresolved, rather than solve one ambiguity by overlooking the other.
When you say “reordering,” are we changing the meaning or the spoken source?

Neither is proposed. Reordering here concerns the order in which target-language material is emitted. Its purpose is to express what can be said early without irreversibly fixing polarity or agent–patient roles before the source supports those commitments. It is not permission to change what the source means.
Is a role-neutral lead-in just filler to consume the lag budget?

No. The proposal is to emit a lead-in as part of the translation, not to insert unrelated filler. It would need to be compatible with the eventual clause meaning while leaving the unresolved commitments open. The proposal does not state how often such wording is available.
Why emit a lead-in at all instead of waiting until both polarity and roles become clear?

Emitting a suitable lead-in is a proposed way to start producing irreversible output without immediately taking the semantic risks that come with committing to polarity or roles. Simply waiting for everything to become clear could consume too much time. The 1.8-second lag budget keeps timing in view, though the proposal does not claim the budget has been achieved.
Does delaying a commitment mean it can be changed after it has been emitted?

No. Delaying means not making that commitment yet. Once the decoder emits a target prefix, the output remains irreversible; later information can guide subsequent words but cannot rewrite an earlier assertion. The proposal tries to make the earlier wording safe enough to stand.
What specifically would go wrong with assigning agent and patient too early?

If later source information establishes the opposite relationship, the emitted target prefix might already say, in effect, that the wrong participant acted or was affected. Further output would not erase that earlier commitment. Role-neutral wording is proposed to avoid making such an assignment before it is warranted.
And if negation arrives late?

An early affirmative commitment could conflict with a later negator. Delaying the polarity commitment means the lead-in should not force that affirmative reading before the source resolves it. The proposal does not say that every late negator can be accommodated this way.
Is the 1.8-second figure the duration of a commit gate?

No gate duration is stated in this proposal. The 1.8 seconds is a *lag budget* for clause-aware reordering and its delayed commitments. It should not be relabeled as a gate setting or presented as a measured lagging result.
Does calling it a lag budget guarantee that actual average lagging will be 1.8 seconds?

No. A budget is a proposed constraint on the approach, not an observed value or a guarantee of performance. The proposal does not provide measured average lagging, a distribution of delays, or results showing that it stays within that budget.
How does the 1.8-second budget relate to the broader below-two-second average-lagging requirement?

The proposal specifies a 1.8-second lag budget while the broader goal requires average lagging below two seconds. The numbers are related as timing constraints, but stating a budget does not establish what measured average lagging will be or that the broader requirement has been met.
If a clause offers no natural role-neutral opening, does this proposal require the decoder to invent one?

No such fallback is specified. The proposal describes using role-neutral lead-ins through clause-aware reordering; it does not claim a suitable lead-in exists for every clause or give a rule for clauses where one cannot be emitted appropriately.
Could we infer that reordering necessarily improves negation and role errors relative to a matched-latency streaming baseline?

No. The proposal describes a way to avoid premature polarity and agent–patient commitments; it reports no error counts or comparison with a baseline. Whether it reduces those errors, and whether it does so while preserving timing and overall quality, remains to be tested.
Does this proposal specify what counts as an acceptable lead-in in every target language?

No. It states the intended property—role-neutral early output that avoids premature polarity and agent–patient commitments—without naming a language pair, a construction, or a linguistic rule that would work universally. A lead-in must still serve as appropriate target output, not merely delay a decision.
Can I summarize the idea as getting some safe translation out early and reserving the meaning-sensitive wording until later, subject to 1.8 seconds of lag?

Yes, if “safe” means the role-neutral lead-in does not itself fix polarity or agent–patient roles that remain unresolved. The precise proposal is clause-aware reordering to emit those lead-ins and delay the two kinds of commitment under a 1.8-second lag budget. It is a proposed approach, not a demonstrated timing or accuracy result.
The open question for clause-aware reordering is this: how can it defer agent–patient and polarity decisions without producing ungrammatical English or exceeding 1.8 seconds?

That is the central constraint on the proposal. It is not enough to postpone the risky words: whatever English is emitted before the roles and polarity are settled must work as English, and the deferral must fit within the 1.8-second lag budget. The question does not yet specify a reordering rule that accomplishes both.
Why is grammatical English an issue if the lead-in avoids assigning roles?

Because avoiding a semantic commitment and forming a grammatical English opening are separate requirements. A sequence might leave the agent and patient unstated but still be awkward or incomplete in a way that cannot be continued naturally. The decoder has to consider whether the early output can stand as the beginning of a well-formed translation, not just whether it avoids an explicit role assignment.
And polarity creates the same sort of problem?

Yes. An English opening can imply an affirmative interpretation even without an explicit statement about negation. Conversely, withholding so much of the clause that polarity remains open could make the English difficult to construct or delay meaningful output. The question is how to defer that decision without either consequence.
Does “grammatical English” require every emitted prefix to be a complete sentence?

Not necessarily. In simultaneous translation, an emitted prefix may be an unfinished beginning that later words complete. The concern is whether it can be continued into grammatical English without retracting or replacing what was already emitted. The question does not define a stricter grammaticality test.
So a prefix could be unfinished but still acceptable if it supports a grammatical continuation?

Conceptually, yes. Being unfinished is different from being unable to form a grammatical sentence when continued. The harder condition here is that the continuation must also preserve the eventual agent–patient assignment and polarity without revising the prefix.
What exactly must the reordering avoid committing to too early?

Two decisions are named: which participant is the agent and which is the patient, and whether the clause conveys positive or negative polarity. Deferring one while inadvertently fixing the other would not resolve the question.
Could it simply omit the agent and patient until their roles are clear?

That describes one way to postpone a role assignment in the abstract, but it does not establish that the resulting English would be grammatical or that the delay would stay within 1.8 seconds. The open question asks how those conditions can be met together, not merely how to leave participants unmentioned.
What if the English wording is grammatical at first but later information forces a different beginning?

Then it has not provided a suitable irreversible prefix. Grammaticality at the moment of emission is insufficient if later role or polarity information would require rewriting that beginning. The intended deferral has to preserve a path to grammatical English *and* the correct meaning after the late information arrives.
Could a translator solve the meaning problem by waiting for the whole clause before saying anything?

Waiting could resolve uncertainty, but this question includes the 1.8-second limit. It does not assume that the whole clause is available within that budget. A response that depends on unrestricted waiting would leave the timing part unanswered.
Is 1.8 seconds a measured delay for this reordering method?
No. It is the lag limit posed in the question. No measured lag or successful reordering outcome is given here.
Should we interpret it as permission to delay every commitment by exactly 1.8 seconds?

No. The question is whether the relevant decisions can be deferred *without exceeding* 1.8 seconds. It does not prescribe a fixed wait of 1.8 seconds for each commitment or define a particular timing schedule.
Does the question require the decoder to make the agent–patient and polarity decisions at the same moment?

It does not specify that. It asks how to defer both decisions while preserving grammatical English and the timing constraint. If one becomes clear before the other, that would still leave the need to avoid a premature commitment on the unresolved dimension; no exact release order is stated.
What is the tension between clause-aware reordering and English word order?

Reordering target material may create room to say something before all source-side distinctions are resolved. But an English beginning cannot be treated as an arbitrary collection of movable words: its order and form have to support a grammatical continuation. The question asks how to use the flexibility that exists without assuming unlimited flexibility.
Can we answer it by naming a particular English lead-in that always works?

Nothing here establishes a universal lead-in. Whether an opening remains grammatical and avoids polarity and agent–patient commitments depends on what the clause ultimately needs to express. Giving a fixed phrase as a guaranteed solution would go beyond the question.
Could the decoder produce words that sound neutral but indirectly imply who acted?

That is precisely a risk the question brings into view. A lead-in is not genuinely role-neutral merely because it omits an overt agent label; its English wording must also avoid conveying an agent–patient assignment that later information could reverse. The same caution applies to implicit positive polarity.
What would count as a satisfactory answer to the question, without claiming we have one yet?

It would explain how clause-aware reordering selects early English that can be continued grammatically while leaving unresolved agent–patient and polarity decisions open, and how the resulting timing stays within 1.8 seconds. This node poses those requirements but provides neither a selection procedure nor evidence that the timing condition is achieved.
Does grammaticality alone tell us whether the final translation preserves the intended meaning?

No. A sentence can be grammatical English while assigning the wrong agent and patient or expressing the wrong polarity. Both grammatical form and faithful meaning matter, in addition to the 1.8-second constraint.
And can correct eventual meaning alone excuse an ungrammatical early output?

Not under this question. It explicitly asks how to defer the meaning-sensitive decisions *without producing ungrammatical English*. An eventual interpretation that is right would not, by itself, answer the grammaticality concern.
So the question remains about finding English prefixes that are grammatical to continue, semantically noncommittal where needed, and timely?

Yes. More precisely, it asks how clause-aware reordering can defer agent–patient and polarity decisions while keeping the English grammatical and not exceeding 1.8 seconds. Those requirements are posed together; no specific solution or result is asserted here.

Here is a hypothesis for the clause-aware reordering question: constrained role-neutral English lead-ins will reduce negation and role errors by at least 20% while preserving at least 95% grammaticality, AL below 1.8 seconds, and baseline COMET.

That is a prediction, not an observed outcome. It proposes that constraining the English lead-ins to avoid premature role commitments can reduce the targeted errors while meeting three other conditions: grammaticality of at least 95%, average lagging below 1.8 seconds, and COMET that preserves the baseline level.

It says the early English wording is not freely chosen just to fill time. It must remain role-neutral and suitable for the translation as the clause unfolds. The hypothesis does not specify the constraints themselves or a procedure for choosing lead-ins.
Does role-neutral mean the lead-in can ignore polarity?

No. The hypothesis targets negation as well as role errors. An opening that avoids naming the agent but irreversibly conveys affirmative polarity could still be wrong if a negator arrives later. The proposed lead-ins are meant to avoid premature meaning commitments relevant to both error types.
Could the decoder emit any grammatical introductory phrase and count that as success?

No. Grammaticality is only one condition. The lead-in must also function as appropriate translation output without committing to an incorrect role or polarity, and the approach must satisfy the stated error, lagging, and COMET conditions. A grammatical phrase that changes or adds meaning would not resolve the underlying problem.
Is the 95% figure a promise that every emitted prefix will be grammatical?

No. The hypothesis sets a grammaticality threshold of at least 95%; it does not predict 100% grammaticality or guarantee that each individual prefix is grammatical. It also does not define a grammaticality assessment procedure.

No. Here, at least 95% refers to grammaticality. A 95%-mass lattice is a different concept: its percentage describes the mass represented in a lattice. This hypothesis is about constrained role-neutral English lead-ins and does not equate the two percentages.
What exactly is being reduced by at least 20%?

Negation and role errors are the targeted errors. The threshold is a relative reduction of at least 20%, not a decrease of 20 percentage points. The hypothesis does not provide error counts or specify an aggregation rule for the two categories.
If negation errors improve but role errors get worse, can we already say the hypothesis holds?

No. The claim explicitly concerns negation and role errors, so a result involving opposite movements would need to be assessed against a stated way of measuring the targeted reduction. This hypothesis supplies no category-specific counts or rule for resolving that situation; we should not declare it satisfied on that basis alone.
Does the hypothesis give a new baseline for that 20% comparison?

It does not name a new comparison system or provide baseline error values. The broader translation goal uses a matched-latency streaming baseline for its error target, but this hypothesis itself states the predicted reduction without detailing a comparison protocol.
What does it mean to preserve baseline COMET?

The predicted overall COMET should not fall below the baseline level. This is a separate quality condition, not a claim that COMET is already known or that it must increase. The hypothesis gives no COMET scores.
Could a 20% reduction in those errors compensate for COMET dropping?

Not under the hypothesis as written. It predicts the error reduction *while* preserving baseline COMET. Similarly, a favorable COMET result alone would not establish the targeted error reduction or the grammaticality and timing conditions.
How strict is the timing condition? Would AL of exactly 1.8 seconds qualify?
No. AL means average lagging, and ‘below 1.8 seconds’ is strict. Exactly 1.8 seconds would not satisfy that part of the hypothesis.
Does AL below 1.8 seconds mean that every lead-in must appear within 1.8 seconds?
No. AL is an average timing measure, not a per-lead-in deadline. The hypothesis does not specify when each individual lead-in must be emitted.
And 1.8 seconds is not a new gate duration?
Correct. This hypothesis gives an AL threshold of less than 1.8 seconds. It does not specify a commit-gate duration or equate a gate setting with measured average lagging.
Why put grammaticality and COMET alongside the targeted errors?

Because deferring role and polarity decisions would not be an adequate solution if the resulting English were frequently ungrammatical or overall translation quality fell. The hypothesis makes the proposed error reduction conditional on maintaining grammaticality, timely output, and baseline COMET rather than treating safer early commitments as the only consideration.
Could a lead-in be grammatical when first emitted but become impossible to continue faithfully after the source resolves?

Yes; grammaticality at the moment of emission would not by itself make an irreversible prefix safe. The eventual continuation must still express the correct polarity and agent–patient relationship without rewriting the lead-in. The hypothesis does not provide a guarantee that this is always possible.
Does the hypothesis claim a grammatical lead-in exists for every clause?
No. It predicts aggregate conditions for the proposed constrained lead-ins but does not assert that every clause admits a suitable opening or specify what to do when one is unavailable.
Can we already say whether this approach achieves its predicted error reduction or grammaticality threshold?

No. There are no results for these constrained lead-ins in the hypothesis. The at-least-20% error reduction, at-least-95% grammaticality, AL below 1.8 seconds, and preservation of baseline COMET all remain predictions to assess.
So the claim is not that we can trade some grammaticality for lower lag?

Right. It specifies both a grammaticality floor of at least 95% and an AL ceiling strictly below 1.8 seconds. One favorable result cannot substitute for missing the other, and both accompany the error-reduction and COMET conditions.
Give me the hypothesis in a form that keeps all four conditions and its uncertainty clear.

The hypothesis is that constrained role-neutral English lead-ins will reduce negation and role errors by at least 20% while achieving at least 95% grammaticality, keeping average lagging below 1.8 seconds, and preserving baseline COMET. Those are predicted outcomes, not reported results.
